question:
A 20-year-old male presents following a knife altercation with a 2-centimeter wound in zone 2 of his
index finger. Clinical examination reveals pain during finger flexion and extension, and exploration
shows a 40% laceration of the flexor tendons. What is the optimal treatment strategy? Answer Choices:
(A) Modified Kessler technique with 4-strand repair (B) Conservative management with splinting only
(C) Primary tendon repair with 3/0 braided suture (D) Trim the frayed tendon edges and begin early
range of motion (E) Delayed primary repair after inflammation subsides (F) Immobilization in flexion for
6 weeks (G) Peritendinous 6/0 and Core 4/0 suture repair (H) Trim the frayed tendon edges and cast in
an intrinsic positive position for 2 weeks (I) Epitendinous running suture repair (J) Tendon graft from
palmaris longus
 A. Peritendinous 6/0 and Core 4/0 suture repair
B. Trim the frayed tendon edges and cast in an intrinsic positive position for 2 weeks
C. Primary tendon repair with 3/0 braided suture
D. Tendon graft from palmaris longus
E. Delayed primary repair after inflammation subsides
F. Trim the frayed tendon edges and begin early range of motion
G. Conservative management with splinting only
H. Immobilization in flexion for 6 weeks
I. Epitendinous running suture repair
J. Modified Kessler technique with 4-strand repair
